items.text: You weren't lazy. Your nervous system reached the limit of what it could carry and did what overloaded systems do: it stopped. Burnout is a capacity problem, not a character problem.
items.rationale: Leads with the accusation autistic people have internalized ('lazy'), then reframes it as physiology. Ends on the sharpest distinction — capacity vs. character — rather than trailing into explanation.

items.text: If your diagnosis felt like grief and relief at the same time — sometimes in the same hour — there's a word for that now. 'Grelief.' Researchers are using it. The community coined it first.
items.rationale: Naming an unnamed experience is the entire point. The beat 'researchers are using it / community coined it first' flips the usual credibility order in a way that respects where the knowledge actually came from.

items.text: For a PDA nervous system, a demand is a threat — even if it's something you want to do. 'Just push through' doesn't work because wanting and feeling safe enough to start are two different things.
items.rationale: The core insight — wanting ≠ safe enough to start — is the sharpest line in this angle. Positions 'just push through' as named bad advice without dunking on whoever gave it.

items.text: If becoming a character is the only way your brain will let you show up, that's not avoidance. That's accommodation. The character earns the dopamine the demand would block.
items.rationale: Lands the mechanism in one sentence without requiring the reader to already know the ADHD-PDA framework. Validates a behavior many people feel sheepish about by naming why it works.

items.text: What you're calling procrastination might be autistic inertia — wanting to move and still not being able to shift states. That's a different thing from ADHD task paralysis. The difference changes what helps.
items.rationale: Opens with the word people already use ('procrastination'), introduces the distinction, closes on the practical implication. The question lives in the reframe rather than a literal '?' — it invites people to place themselves.
items.sensitivity_flag: Uses 'might be' appropriately, but a minority of readers could read this as nudging toward self-diagnosis. The hedge is sufficient; watch replies for misreads.

items.text: 70% of neurodivergent workers still fear disclosing at work in 2026. What would actually need to change for that number to move?
items.rationale: The stat does the setup cleanly. The question is genuinely open — no implied answer — which separates it from engagement bait. Short on purpose; the question is the whole post.

items.text: Late diagnosis emotions: relief, grief, and — for a lot of people — fury. Decades of being misread, dismissed, misdiagnosed. The anger is valid. It doesn't mean you're not also grateful.
items.rationale: Names the emotion the dominant late-diagnosis narrative leaves out. The last line pre-empts the 'but you should be thankful' redirect without being defensive about it.

items.text: 'Put your shoes on' is a demand. 'The shoes are by the door and we leave at 4' is information. That difference is everything for a PDA nervous system.
items.rationale: Concrete before/after does more work than any explanation. Immediately usable today, no diagnosis or professional needed. The specificity is exactly why practical posts like this get saved.

items.text: What if demand avoidance isn't defiance — it's a part of you that learned the only way to stay safe was to stay in control? That reframe changes how you work with it rather than against it.
items.rationale: Carries the IFS 'protective parts' framing without requiring the reader to know IFS. The pivot from 'against it' to 'with it' lands the therapeutic implication without prescribing a treatment path.

items.text: Autistic burnout can strip away skills you've had for years — conversation, cooking, getting to work. That's not laziness returning. That's the nervous system rationing what's left.
items.rationale: Targets the specific, under-discussed feature of autistic burnout — skill regression — that many people don't expect and can't explain. Concrete examples make it recognizable rather than abstract.

items.text: 70% of neurodivergent workers fear disclosing. 70% don't know what they're entitled to. Those aren't separate problems. You can't ask for what you don't know you're allowed to have.
items.rationale: The parallel 70%/70% stat is striking on its own. The final line draws the connection explicitly without editorializing. Different angle on the same source as post 6 — pairs without repeating.

items.text: Declarative language works on yourself too. 'I need to write this report' is a demand. 'It's 2pm and the doc is open' is just information. Smaller ask, lower threat, more access.
items.rationale: Extends the declarative language concept beyond parenting into adult self-support — a less-covered application. Keeps the before/after structure that makes the parenting version immediately useful.
